title: CPSC 541 - Chapter 2: Requirements from the Customer's Perspective

questions.question: Which statement best describes a customer in the context of software requirements?
options: A customer is only the person who operates the software directly and never anyone who merely receives its outputs.
A customer is only the person who pays for the product and never anyone who uses it or benefits from it.
A customer is anyone who benefits from, requests, pays for, uses, or receives output generated by the product.
A customer is only the project manager who schedules the work and never anyone who will use or fund the product.
A customer is only a member of the development team who writes code and never an outside user or sponsor.
A customer is only a programmer who writes source code for the product and never a person who uses it.
questions.explanation: The chapter uses a broad definition of customer. Customers can include people who benefit from the product, request or pay for it, use it, or receive its output.

reference.excerpt: Customers are a subset of stakeholders. A customer is an individual or organization that derives either direct or indirect benefit from a product. Software customers could request, pay for, select, specify, use, or receive the output generated by a software product.
reference.lecture: Having baseline is important because it is the foundation of future development in terms of functionality, cost, and time, etc. So in this chapter, in summary, we have looked at the requirements from the customer point of view. Initially, we have identified what are the meanings of the customers, and then look at 10 rights and 10 responsibilities of customers.

questions.question: Every customer is an important stakeholder in the software project.
questions.explanation: Customers have an interest in or dependence on the intended product and therefore are important stakeholders.

reference.excerpt: Customers are a subset of stakeholders. A customer is an individual or organization that derives either direct or indirect benefit from a product.
reference.lecture: Welcome to chapter 2. In this chapter, we look at the requirements from the customer's point of view. First of all, who are the customers? There are multiple understandings who the customers are, and slide 2 shows possible meanings of these customers. An important thing is that all of them have interests in or dependence on the intended product.

questions.question: A department manager never directly uses a reporting system but receives a weekly report generated by it. According to Chapter 2, can this person still be considered a customer?
questions.explanation: A person who receives and benefits from the product's output can be considered a customer.

reference.excerpt: Indirect users might receive outputs from the system without touching it themselves, such as a warehouse manager who receives an automatic report of daily warehouse activities by email.
reference.lecture: And then we talked about the baseline, which is created once the customer signs off the requirements, and the importance of the baseline.

questions.question: Why is the customer-developer relationship important?
options: Customers are responsible for writing the application's source code, so the relationship is mainly a programming partnership.
Excellent requirements depend heavily on effective collaboration between customers and the developers who will build the product.
Developers should allow customers to make every technical design decision so that a requirements partnership is unnecessary.
Customers alone determine the programming language and tools, which makes an ongoing customer-developer relationship unnecessary.
Developers do not need written requirements when communication is already good, so the relationship can replace specification work.
Customers are responsible for performing all software testing, and that testing duty is why the customer-developer relationship matters.
questions.explanation: The chapter emphasizes that excellent requirements come from effective collaboration between customers and developers.

reference.excerpt: This chapter addresses the customer-development relationship that is so critical to software project success. Good software depends on good requirements, and good requirements depend on communication between customers and developers.
reference.lecture: So it is needless to say that developers should have excellent relationships in order to have excellent requirements, which then will have influence on excellence of the product. As we know that many products have failed and left unsatisfied customers because of the lack of clear communication between developers and customers. So the job of requirements analysts is to identify and listen to the customers and also satisfy them before moving forward.

questions.question: According to the chapter, excellent software is strongly influenced by which two things?
options: Excellent software comes mainly from a large budget and a large team rather than from requirements quality and design.
Excellent software is strongly influenced by excellent requirements together with a well-executed design of the solution.
Excellent software comes mainly from fast programming and minimal documentation rather than from careful requirements work.
Excellent software comes mainly from adopting new technology and cloud hosting rather than from requirements and design.
Excellent software comes mainly from automated testing and artificial intelligence rather than from requirements collaboration.
Excellent software comes mainly from a short schedule and few stakeholders rather than from requirements and design quality.
questions.explanation: The slides state that excellent software comes from well-executed design and excellent requirements.

reference.excerpt: Good software depends on good requirements, and good requirements depend on communication between customers and developers.
reference.lecture: So it is needless to say that developers should have excellent relationships in order to have excellent requirements, which then will have influence on excellence of the product. As we know that many products have failed and left unsatisfied customers because of the lack of clear communication between developers and customers. So the job of requirements analysts is to identify and listen to the customers and also satisfy them before moving forward.

questions.question: What is one major cause of dissatisfied customers discussed in Chapter 2?
options: Customers become dissatisfied mainly because developers chose the wrong programming language for implementing the product.
Lack of clear communication between customers and developers is a major cause of dissatisfied customers discussed in the chapter.
Customers become dissatisfied mainly because the team performed more testing than was necessary before the product was released.
Customers become dissatisfied mainly because analysts documented requirements in writing instead of relying on informal conversation.
Customers become dissatisfied mainly because the project included too many stakeholder interviews before programming work began.
Customers become dissatisfied mainly because developers followed a defined requirements process instead of starting to code immediately.
questions.explanation: Poor communication can create misunderstandings between what customers need and what developers build.

reference.excerpt: Without adequate customer involvement, the inescapable outcome at the end of the project is an expectation gap, a gulf between what customers really need and what developers deliver based on what they heard at the beginning of the project.

So the job of requirements analysts is to identify and listen to the customers and also satisfy them before moving forward.

questions.question: One role of a requirements analyst is to identify the appropriate customers and listen to their needs before development proceeds.
questions.explanation: The professor emphasizes identifying and listening to customers as an important responsibility of requirements analysts.

reference.excerpt: Business analysts need to collaborate with users to reach that deeper understanding. The job of requirements analysts is to identify and listen to the customers before moving forward.

questions.question: Which of the following are rights of the software customer? Select all that apply.
options: Customers have the right to expect analysts to speak the customer's language rather than unnecessary technical jargon.
Customers have the right to expect analysts to learn the customer's business and the objectives of the work.
Customers have the right to expect analysts to document the requirements in an appropriate written or graphical form.
Customers have the right to expect analysts to explain requirements practices and the work products they produce.
Customers have the right to expect analysts to treat them respectfully and to work in a professional manner.
Customers have the right to require developers to accept every requested change without discussing cost or schedule.
questions.explanation: The first five are customer rights. Customers do not have the right to force every change into the project without evaluating its impact.

reference.excerpt: You have the right to expect BAs to speak your language, learn about your business and your objectives, record requirements in an appropriate form, receive explanations of requirements practices and deliverables, and expect an environment of mutual respect.
reference.lecture: In order to have this well-connected relationship between customers and analysts, Uyghur identifies 10 so-called bill of rights and 10 customers' responsibilities. Slides 4 to 7 show the rights of customers, that is, what the customer can expect from the analysts. And slides 7 to 9 show the responsibilities of customers, and most of them are obvious, but the point is that the customer should spend time and effort to understand and to be active in all phases of requirements analysis.

questions.question: What does it mean when the customer has the right to expect analysts to 'speak your language'?
options: The analyst must use the customer's preferred programming language when discussing how the software will be implemented.
The analyst should communicate in understandable business terms instead of forcing customers to wade through technical jargon.
The analyst must be able to speak every human language that any stakeholder on the project might possibly prefer to use.
The analyst should communicate only through diagrams and must never discuss requirements with customers in spoken language.
The analyst must allow the customer to write the application's source code so that technical jargon is no longer needed.
The analyst should avoid asking clarifying questions so that customers are never asked to explain their own business terms.
questions.explanation: Analysts should communicate in language the customer understands rather than expecting customers to understand specialized software terminology.

reference.excerpt: Requirements discussions should center on your business needs and tasks, using business vocabulary. You shouldn't have to wade through technical jargon when talking with BAs.
reference.lecture: In order to have this well-connected relationship between customers and analysts, Uyghur identifies 10 so-called bill of rights and 10 customers' responsibilities. questions.question: A business analyst spends time learning how a hospital processes patients before defining requirements for a hospital system. Which customer right does this support?
options: Customers have the right to expect analysts to learn the customer's business domain and the objectives of the work.
Customers have the right to expect that every approved requirement will remain unchanged for the rest of the project.
Customers have the right to expect that they themselves will write the complete software requirements specification document.
Customers have the right to expect developers to ignore technical feasibility when deciding which requested features to build.
Customers have the right to expect immediate implementation of every requested feature before requirements have been clarified.
Customers have the right to expect that they will approve source code instead of reviewing documented requirements with analysts.
questions.explanation: Customers have the right to expect analysts to understand their business domain and objectives.

reference.excerpt: By interacting with you to elicit requirements, the BAs can better understand your business tasks and how the system fits into your world. This will help developers create a solution that meets your needs.

questions.question: Customers have the right to expect analysts to convert information they provide into written or graphical requirements specifications.
questions.explanation: Translating customer information into useful written or graphical requirements is one of the listed customer rights.

reference.excerpt: The ultimate deliverable from this analysis is a refined set of requirements stored in some appropriate form, such as a software requirements specification document. Requirements should be written and organized in a way that you find easy to understand.

questions.question: Why should analysts explain requirements work products to customers?
options: Analysts should explain requirements work products so customers understand what they are reviewing and later agreeing to.
Analysts should explain requirements work products so customers can replace the developers and implement the system themselves.
Analysts should explain requirements work products so that those requirements no longer need any further validation or review.
Analysts should explain requirements work products so developers can stop creating documentation once the explanation is given.
Analysts should explain requirements work products so project managers can avoid estimating cost and schedule for the work.
Analysts should explain requirements work products so that source code can be written immediately without further analysis.
questions.explanation: Customers need to understand the requirements artifacts so they can meaningfully review, clarify, and eventually approve them.

reference.excerpt: The BA should explain the practices he's recommending and explain what information goes into each deliverable. Your review of these specifications and other requirements representations helps to ensure that they accurately represent your needs.

questions.question: Which behavior is expected from an analyst when working with customers?
options: An analyst should dismiss customer concerns whenever those concerns are difficult to address during requirements discussions.
An analyst should be respectful, collaborative, and professional when working with customers on the project's requirements.
An analyst should avoid proposing alternatives so customers never have to compare different ways to meet a business need.
An analyst should make all business decisions for the customer so the customer does not need to stay involved in the work.
An analyst should refuse to explain technical concepts so customers are not asked to understand any part of the solution.
An analyst should accept every customer request without evaluation so impact on cost and schedule is never discussed.
questions.explanation: Respectful and collaborative behavior is explicitly included in the customer's bill of rights.

reference.excerpt: Customers who participate in requirements development have the right to expect BAs and developers to treat them with respect and to appreciate the time they are investing in the project's success.

questions.question: A customer asks for a complicated feature. The analyst proposes a simpler alternative that meets the same business need. Is this consistent with the customer's bill of rights?
questions.explanation: Customers have the right to hear alternatives for requirements and possible implementations.

reference.excerpt: You have the right to hear ideas and alternatives for your requirements and for their solution. A creative BA also adds value by proposing new capabilities that customers haven't even envisioned.

questions.question: Customers should be allowed to describe characteristics that would make the product easy and enjoyable to use.
questions.explanation: The customer's bill of rights includes expressing usability characteristics and expectations.

reference.excerpt: You can expect BAs to ask you about characteristics of the software that go beyond your functional needs. These characteristics, or quality attributes, make the software easier or more pleasant to use.

questions.question: Why might an analyst suggest adjusting a requirement so an existing component can be reused?
options: An analyst suggests reuse adjustments so that all of the customer's original requirements can be eliminated from the project.
An analyst suggests reuse adjustments to potentially reduce development effort, calendar time, or cost for the planned product.
An analyst suggests reuse adjustments so the team can avoid talking to customers about what the product still needs to do.
An analyst suggests reuse adjustments so the written requirements can remain ambiguous and open to later reinterpretation.
An analyst suggests reuse adjustments so the project can eliminate the need to test the product before it is delivered.
An analyst suggests reuse adjustments so that future requirements changes can be prevented for the remainder of the project.
questions.explanation: The slides state that customers should receive opportunities to adjust requirements to permit component reuse.

reference.excerpt: The BA might know of existing software components that come close to addressing some need you described. Adjusting your requirements when sensible reuse opportunities are available saves time and money.

questions.question: If a customer proposes a change after requirements have been agreed upon, what information should the developer provide?
options: After a change is proposed, the developer should say only whether the developer personally likes or dislikes the requested change.
After a change is proposed, the developer should provide credible cost and schedule impacts along with possible tradeoffs.
After a change is proposed, the developer should provide only the new source code that will implement the requested change.
After a change is proposed, the developer should guarantee that the change will have no impact on cost, schedule, or scope.
After a change is proposed, the developer should implement it immediately and report impacts only after the work is finished.
After a change is proposed, the developer should reject it automatically because an agreed specification can never be changed.
questions.explanation: Customers have the right to understand the realistic cost, schedule, and tradeoff implications of changes.

reference.excerpt: Change always has a price. Sometimes adding a new function demands trade-offs with other functions or with the project's schedule or budget.
reference.lecture: Once the requirements are signed off, then this established so-called baseline of the requirements, this represents basically the contract between the customer and developer, which needs to be managed or changed at a later time. And any changes, obviously, after the baseline has been established, change costs money and time and scope, and the customer needs to understand that, so make sure that they read before they sign it off. And developers need to realize there's something that she or he has to deliver.

questions.question: According to the customer's bill of rights, what system should the customer ultimately expect to receive?
options: The customer should ultimately expect to receive whatever system the developers prefer to build, regardless of agreed needs.
The customer should ultimately expect a system that contains every feature that anyone ever mentioned during the project.
The customer should ultimately expect a system that satisfies the customer's communicated and agreed-upon functional needs.
The customer should ultimately expect a system that uses the newest available technology, even if that was never agreed.
The customer should ultimately expect a system that never changes after delivery, regardless of later business needs.
The customer should ultimately expect a system that requires no maintenance after it is delivered to the customer organization.
questions.explanation: The developers are expected to deliver the needs that were communicated and agreed upon.

reference.excerpt: You have the right to receive a system that meets your functional needs and quality expectations. This can happen only if you clearly communicate the information that will let developers build the right product and the parties reach agreement.

questions.question: Which of the following are customer responsibilities? Select all that apply.
options: Customers have a responsibility to educate developers about the business and the specialized terminology used there.
Customers have a responsibility to spend the time needed to provide requirements and to clarify them when asked.
Customers have a responsibility to provide specific and precise information when describing what the product must do.
Customers have a responsibility to make timely decisions about requirements so the project can continue to move forward.
Customers have a responsibility to review requirements documents and to evaluate prototypes of the intended product.
Customers have a responsibility to avoid communicating changes until the end of the project so developers are not interrupted.
questions.explanation: Customers are expected to actively participate throughout requirements development. Changes should be communicated promptly, not hidden.

The customer is failing to write the implementation code, which the chapter lists as a required customer responsibility.
The customer is failing to choose the team's programming language, which the chapter lists as a required customer responsibility.

The customer is failing to execute all product tests, which the chapter lists as a required customer responsibility.

questions.question: Why should customers be specific and precise when describing requirements?
options: Customers should be specific and precise when describing requirements so misunderstanding and ambiguity can be reduced.
Customers should be specific and precise so developers will work faster regardless of the quality of the resulting product.
Customers should be specific and precise so the team can remove the need to validate requirements before construction begins.
Customers should be specific and precise so analysts no longer need to document the requirements in a written specification.
Customers should be specific and precise so every requirement becomes permanent and can never be changed later in the project.
Customers should be specific and precise so the team can eliminate the need to prioritize requirements during analysis.
questions.explanation: Specific and precise input reduces ambiguity and helps create a shared understanding between customers and developers.

reference.excerpt: At some point, someone must resolve the ambiguities and imprecisions. You're the best person to make those decisions. Otherwise, you're relying on the BA or developers to guess correctly.

questions.question: Why are timely customer decisions important during requirements engineering?
options: Timely customer decisions are important because delayed decisions can prevent the project from moving forward with confidence.
Timely customer decisions are important because they allow developers to avoid writing requirements for the planned product.
Timely customer decisions are important because they guarantee that approved requirements will never change later in the project.
Timely customer decisions are important because they eliminate development costs once a decision has been recorded.
Timely customer decisions are important because they allow customers to control the source code the developers will write.
Timely customer decisions are important because they replace the need to establish a requirements baseline for the project.
questions.explanation: The requirements process often depends on customer decisions. Delays can block development or leave unresolved issues.

reference.excerpt: Customers who are authorized to make such decisions must do so promptly when asked. Developers often can't proceed with confidence until you render your decision, so time spent waiting for an answer can delay progress.

questions.question: A developer estimates that a requested feature will require six additional weeks. According to the customer's responsibilities, what should the customer do?
options: The customer should assume the developer is exaggerating and should insist that the feature still fit the original schedule.
The customer should respect the developer's cost and feasibility assessment and then discuss possible tradeoffs for the work.
The customer should demand that the requested feature be completed without any change to the agreed schedule or budget.
The customer should immediately replace the developer for reporting that the requested feature will take additional time.
The customer should ignore the estimate and treat the six-week assessment as irrelevant to the requirements decision.
The customer should remove the requirements baseline so the extra work does not have to be evaluated or negotiated.
questions.explanation: Customers have a responsibility to respect credible assessments of cost and technical feasibility.

The customer, working in collaboration with the development team, has a responsibility to help establish realistic priorities.

questions.question: A customer discovers that a business process has changed. When should the customer communicate the change to the development team?
options: The customer should communicate the business-process change to the development team as soon as the change is discovered.
The customer should communicate the business-process change only after the finished product has already been released.
The customer should communicate the business-process change only during final testing, near the end of development work.

questions.question: Why should customers follow the project's defined change process?
options: Customers should follow the change process so that no requirement is ever allowed to change after it has been written.
Customers should follow the change process so changes are evaluated, tracked, and incorporated in a controlled way.
Customers should follow the change process so developers can reject every proposed change without analyzing its impact.
Customers should follow the change process so customers are prevented from participating in later requirements decisions.
Customers should follow the change process so the team can eliminate cost estimates when a change is later requested.
Customers should follow the change process so the project can avoid establishing a requirements baseline altogether.
questions.explanation: A controlled change process prevents requirements changes from creating unmanaged cost, schedule, and scope problems.

reference.excerpt: To minimize the negative impact of changes, follow the project's defined change control process. This ensures that requested changes are not lost, the impact of each change is analyzed, and all proposed changes are considered in a consistent way.

questions.question: What is one common problem with requirements signoff?

Developers are no longer allowed to communicate with customers after the requirements specification has been signed off.
All product testing must be completed before anyone is permitted to sign off on the project's requirements specification.
The product must already be finished and delivered before customers are asked to sign off on the requirements specification.
Customers become responsible for writing the implementation code as soon as they have signed the requirements specification.
questions.explanation: The slides warn that customers sometimes sign requirements specifications without actually reading and understanding them.

reference.excerpt: One problem is the customer representative who regards signing off as a meaningless ritual. This can lead to future problems when that individual wants to change the requirements or is surprised by what is delivered: 'I signed off on the requirements, but I didn't have time to read them all.'
reference.lecture: Once the requirements are signed off, then this established so-called baseline of the requirements, this represents basically the contract between the customer and developer, which needs to be managed or changed at a later time. And any changes, obviously, after the baseline has been established, change costs money and time and scope, and the customer needs to understand that, so make sure that they read before they sign it off. And developers need to realize there's something that she or he has to deliver.

questions.question: Another signoff problem occurs when developers treat an approved requirements specification as:
options: Developers treat an approved specification as a temporary draft that has no importance for later design or construction work.
Developers treat an approved specification as something permanently fixed that can never be changed for the rest of the project.
Developers treat an approved specification as a source-code repository that already contains the implementation of the product.
Developers treat an approved specification as a testing document only and not as an agreement about product requirements.
Developers treat an approved specification as a budget report that records spending rather than an agreement about requirements.
Developers treat an approved specification as a user manual that already describes how people should operate the finished product.
questions.explanation: The chapter warns against treating the signed specification as 'cast in stone.' Requirements will change.

reference.excerpt: Equally problematic is the development manager who views sign-off as a way to freeze the requirements. Whenever a change request comes along he can protest, 'But you signed off on these requirements, so that's what we're building.'

And developers need to realize there's something that she or he has to deliver.

questions.question: It is realistic to expect that every requirement will be completely known before development begins.
questions.explanation: The slides explicitly state that all requirements cannot possibly be known that early and that requirements will change.

reference.excerpt: Both of these attitudes ignore the reality that it's impossible to know all the requirements early in the project and that requirements will undoubtedly change over time.

questions.question: What is a requirements baseline?
options: A requirements baseline is only a temporary conversation between a customer and a developer about possible product ideas.
A requirements baseline is a snapshot of a stable, controlled, and agreed-upon set of requirements at a point in time.
A requirements baseline is a list of future programming languages that the team might consider for later implementation work.
A requirements baseline is a collection of rejected requirements that stakeholders have already decided not to implement.
A requirements baseline is a backup copy of the source code that developers store after each construction increment is finished.
A requirements baseline is a testing benchmark that records how quickly the team can execute the product's automated tests.
questions.explanation: The baseline converts fluid work-in-progress into an agreed-upon and controlled specification at a particular point in time.

reference.excerpt: A requirements baseline is a set of requirements that has been reviewed and agreed upon and serves as the basis for further development. It is a snapshot of the requirements agreement at a point in time.
reference.lecture: Having baseline is important because it is the foundation of future development in terms of functionality, cost, and time, etc. So in this chapter, in summary, we have looked at the requirements from the customer point of view. Initially, we have identified what are the meanings of the customers, and then look at 10 rights and 10 responsibilities of customers.

questions.question: What does establishing a baseline do to requirements work that was previously fluid and changing?
options: Establishing a baseline deletes the earlier requirements work so the team can start specification over with a blank document.
Establishing a baseline turns previously fluid work into a stable, controlled, and agreed-upon specification for further development.
Establishing a baseline makes the requirements impossible to change, even when the business later needs a controlled adjustment.
Establishing a baseline converts the agreed requirements directly into source code so developers no longer implement from a spec.
Establishing a baseline moves the unfinished requirements directly into testing so construction can be skipped entirely.
Establishing a baseline makes the customer responsible for implementing the product instead of leaving that work to developers.
questions.explanation: A baseline creates an agreed reference point from which future requirements changes can be managed.

reference.excerpt: A requirements baseline is a set of requirements that has been reviewed and agreed upon and serves as the basis for further development. After the decision makers define a baseline, the BA should place the requirements under change control.
reference.lecture: Once the requirements are signed off, then this established so-called baseline of the requirements, this represents basically the contract between the customer and developer, which needs to be managed or changed at a later time. And any changes, obviously, after the baseline has been established, change costs money and time and scope, and the customer needs to understand that, so make sure that they read before they sign it off. And developers need to realize there's something that she or he has to deliver.

questions.question: After a baseline is established, requirements may still change.
questions.explanation: A baseline does not freeze requirements forever. Changes are still possible but must be managed.

reference.excerpt: I agree to make future changes in this baseline through the project's defined change process. I realize that changes might require us to renegotiate cost, resource, and schedule commitments.
reference.lecture: Once the requirements are signed off, then this established so-called baseline of the requirements, this represents basically the contract between the customer and developer, which needs to be managed or changed at a later time. And any changes, obviously, after the baseline has been established, change costs money and time and scope, and the customer needs to understand that, so make sure that they read before they sign it off. And developers need to realize there's something that she or he has to deliver.

questions.question: After a baseline is established, a customer requests several major new features. What must the customer understand?
options: After the baseline, requested major features must always be added at no additional cost to the project's budget or schedule.
After the baseline, changes can require renegotiation of cost, schedule, functionality, or scope before they are accepted.
After the baseline, the team must ignore the baseline so that new features can be added without evaluating their impact.
After the baseline, developers are obligated to work unpaid overtime whenever the customer requests several major new features.
After the baseline, newly requested features automatically replace the existing agreed requirements without any further review.
After the baseline, the project deadline can never move, even if the customer later adds several major new features.
questions.explanation: Changes after the baseline can affect project commitments and may require tradeoffs or renegotiation.

reference.excerpt: I agree to make future changes in this baseline through the project's defined change process. I realize that changes might require us to renegotiate cost, resource, and schedule commitments.
reference.lecture: Once the requirements are signed off, then this established so-called baseline of the requirements, this represents basically the contract between the customer and developer, which needs to be managed or changed at a later time. And any changes, obviously, after the baseline has been established, change costs money and time and scope, and the customer needs to understand that, so make sure that they read before they sign it off. And developers need to realize there's something that she or he has to deliver.

questions.question: What should the developer understand about an established requirements baseline?
options: Developers should understand the baseline as merely a suggestion that they may follow or ignore during later construction work.
Developers should understand the baseline as a promise to perform according to the agreed requirements for that portion of work.
Developers should understand the baseline as a way to eliminate the customer's involvement after the specification is approved.
Developers should understand the baseline as a replacement for the project schedule rather than as an agreed requirements snapshot.
Developers should understand the baseline as a freeze that prevents all future changes, even through the defined change process.
Developers should understand the baseline as an agreement that applies only to testers and not to the developers themselves.
questions.explanation: The slides describe the baseline as a commitment by the developer to deliver the agreed-upon product.

reference.excerpt: I agree that this set of requirements represents our best understanding of the requirements for the next portion of this project and that the solution described will meet our needs as we understand them today.
reference.lecture: Once the requirements are signed off, then this established so-called baseline of the requirements, this represents basically the contract between the customer and developer, which needs to be managed or changed at a later time. And any changes, obviously, after the baseline has been established, change costs money and time and scope, and the customer needs to understand that, so make sure that they read before they sign it off. And developers need to realize there's something that she or he has to deliver.

questions.question: Why does a requirements baseline increase stakeholder confidence?
options: A baseline increases confidence because it guarantees that the delivered software will contain no defects of any kind.
A baseline increases confidence by giving stakeholders a controlled agreement about scope and how later changes will be handled.
A baseline increases confidence because it guarantees that the project will have an unlimited budget for every requested feature.
A baseline increases confidence because it prevents users from requesting any further changes after construction has started.
A baseline increases confidence because it eliminates the need to continue the requirements process after the snapshot is taken.
A baseline increases confidence because it allows developers to ignore customers once the agreed specification has been signed.
questions.explanation: The baseline provides a shared reference point and helps prevent uncontrolled changes and misunderstandings.

reference.excerpt: A meaningful baselining process gives all the major stakeholders confidence. Customer management is confident that the project scope won't explode out of control, because customers manage the scope change decisions.
reference.lecture: Once the requirements are signed off, then this established so-called baseline of the requirements, this represents basically the contract between the customer and developer, which needs to be managed or changed at a later time. And any changes, obviously, after the baseline has been established, change costs money and time and scope, and the customer needs to understand that, so make sure that they read before they sign it off. And developers need to realize there's something that she or he has to deliver.

questions.question: Which stakeholder confidence benefits are associated with having a requirements baseline? Select all that apply.
options: Customer managers gain confidence that project scope will not grow uncontrollably because change decisions stay managed.
Users gain confidence that developers will work with them toward the right system even if some needs were missed early.
Development managers gain confidence that customers will consider cost, schedule, and functionality tradeoffs as partners.
Analysts gain confidence that requirements changes will be managed so they do not create uncontrolled project chaos.
Developers are guaranteed that requirements will never change again after the baseline has been established for the release.
Customers no longer need to participate in requirements work after the baseline has been established for the project.
questions.explanation: The chapter presents the baseline as a way to create confidence among customer managers, users, development managers, and analysts while still allowing controlled change.

reference.excerpt: Customer management is confident that the project scope won't explode out of control, because customers manage the scope change decisions. User representatives have confidence that the development team will work with them to deliver the right solution.
